mastery_questions: Aggregate the data to the customer level: for each Customer ID, compute total Sales, total Profit, order count, and average discount. Paste the first 5 rows and the row count. Now rank customers by total Profit descending and assign segments: VIP (top 10%), High Value (next 20%), Medium (next 40%), Low (bottom 30%). Use PERCENTRANK or NTILE logic. Paste the segment count and aggregate profit for each segment.

Compute the Pareto curve. Sort customers by total profit descending. Add a cumulative profit column (running sum). Add a cumulative percentage of total profit column (cumulative / grand total). Add a cumulative percentage of customers column (row number / total customers). Find the row where cumulative profit percentage first exceeds 80%. Paste that row. What percentage of customers does it represent? Is it above or below 80/20?

Build the segment profile table: for each segment, compute average order count, average order value (Sales / order count), average discount received, and Category mix (percentage of orders in each Category). Paste the table. Write two sentences comparing VIPs to Low Value customers on at least two dimensions -- specifically, do VIPs receive lower or higher average discounts? This connection between segmentation and discount policy is the finding that ties weeks 3 and 4 together.

Build the Pareto chart: a combination chart with cumulative customer percentage on the x-axis, a bar chart showing each customer's profit contribution, and a line showing the cumulative profit percentage. The 80% line on the y-axis is the key visual reference. Paste the chart. A reader should be able to identify the 80/20 point from the chart without reading the underlying table.

Write the memo update: one new paragraph stating the three specific characteristics that distinguish VIP customers from Low Value customers, with numbers for each. Do not write "VIPs spend more" -- write "VIP customers place an average of 14 orders per year versus 2 for Low Value customers, at an average order value of $847 versus $312, and receive an average discount of 8% versus 24%." Paste the paragraph.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the SUMIF formula for aggregating order-level data to the customer level. It is a multi-column SUMIF with customer ID as the criteria and multiple columns to aggregate -- mechanical but error-prone to write manually. Verify the output for 3 spot-check customers. Do NOT ask Claude to write the memo paragraph comparing VIPs to Low Value customers -- that comparison requires reading the actual numbers from your segment table, not generating plausible-sounding ones.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your audience for the CLV analysis is the marketing team. They want to know: 'Who do we send the next campaign to?' Lead your memo update with 3 specific named customer segments and the action for each.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building the segmentation, compute the total number of unique customers in the dataset and the total profit. Then estimate: if the 80/20 rule holds exactly, how many customers are in the top 20% and what is their aggregate profit? Write those two numbers down. The comparison between your estimate and the actual Pareto calculation is informative -- most datasets are more unequal than 80/20, and a few are less.
common_mistakes: Computing customer total profit at the order level instead of the customer level. A customer with 20 orders appears 20 times in the raw data -- aggregate to the customer level first with a SUMIF or groupby before segmenting.

Using revenue instead of profit for CLV segmentation in a dataset where margins vary widely. A customer who buys heavily discounted Furniture may have high revenue and negative profit contribution. Profit-based segmentation gives a more accurate picture of true customer value.

Assigning segment labels that overlap (top 10%, top 20%, etc.) instead of non-overlapping ranges (top 10%, 10-30%, 30-70%, 70-100%). Double-check that every customer appears in exactly one segment and the segment percentages sum to 100%.

Charting the Pareto curve with profit on the x-axis instead of cumulative customer count. The convention is customers on the x-axis, cumulative profit on the y-axis -- the curve bends toward the top-left, showing that the left portion of customers drives a disproportionate share of profit.

Ignoring the Low Value segment in the analysis. The finding about VIPs is interesting. The finding about the Low Value segment -- specifically whether they are loss-making at high discounts -- is actionable.
weeks.debug_help: The PERCENTRANK-based segmentation fails if you are using PERCENTRANK on the profit column directly, because PERCENTRANK assigns the same rank to ties. For customer segmentation, you want RANK.EQ or RANK.AVG on the sorted profit column, then divide by total customers. The cleaner Excel approach: sort by profit descending, add a rank column (=ROW()-1, adjusted for header), then use IF nested on the rank fraction. In Python: df['percentile'] = df['profit'].rank(pct=True) and cut into segments with pd.qcut or pd.cut.
stretch: Compute the retention rate by segment: of customers who placed an order in 2016, what percentage placed at least one order in 2017? Compute separately for VIPs and Low Value customers. The retention rate difference by segment is one of the strongest arguments for differential treatment of customer groups.

Map the VIP customers by State using a geographic pivot table. Are the VIP customers concentrated in specific states? If so, does the regional concentration match the high-performing regions from week 1? Connecting the customer analysis to the geographic analysis is the kind of multi-dimensional insight that distinguishes a senior analyst's work.

Compute RFM scores (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) for the customer base as an alternative segmentation approach. Score each customer 1-5 on each dimension, then combine the scores. Compare the RFM segments to the profit-based segments. Where do they agree and where do they disagree? The disagreements are the most instructive cases.

weeks.title: Superstore v0.4: SQL version
weeks.context:
You have done the Superstore analysis twice: once in Excel, once in Python. This week you do it in SQL -- the language that runs every serious data organisation's analytical infrastructure. Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, and every other data warehouse accepts SQL as input. Pandas is useful when you can fit the data in memory on your laptop. SQL is what you use when the data lives somewhere else and you cannot.

The SQL version of the Superstore analysis has a specific goal: every pivot table and calculated metric from weeks 1 through 4 should be expressible as a SQL query that you can run against a database. You will load the Superstore CSV into a local SQLite database and write queries.sql with at least eight queries -- one for each of the main analytical questions. The queries should be readable: comments above each one, clear aliases, formatted with line breaks.

CTEs (Common Table Expressions, the WITH ... AS clause) are the SQL equivalent of naming an intermediate result in Excel. Instead of a formula that references a formula that references another formula, you name each step: WITH customer_totals AS (...), then segment_ranks AS (...), then SELECT FROM segment_ranks. CTEs make complex SQL readable and debuggable, and they are the standard pattern in every modern analytics SQL style guide.

Self-joins are how you compute year-over-year comparisons in SQL. You join the orders table to itself, matching on Category and the year, and compute the ratio between the two year's values. It is not intuitive until you see it once, and once you see it it is the natural way to express "compare this year to last year."

By Sunday: queries.sql committed to the Superstore repo with at least eight queries, every query producing a result that matches the corresponding Excel or Python output, and a brief comment above each query explaining what question it answers.

days.title: SELECT — read columns from a table
days.summary: The language of every data warehouse. Today: SELECT … FROM … LIMIT, and load Superstore into SQL.

items.title: SELECT — read columns from a table
items.body:
## What it is
**SQL** asks a database for data. The core statement: `SELECT` the columns you want `FROM` a table. `*` means all columns; `LIMIT` peeks at a few rows.

## Why it matters
You've done Superstore in Excel and pandas. SQL is the third — and the one every serious data org runs on (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, Databricks all speak SQL). Same questions, but it scales to billions of rows that never fit on your laptop.

## Setup (free, in-browser)
Go to **sqliteonline.com**, click *Import* → upload your Superstore CSV → name the table `superstore`. No install.

## Examples
```sql
-- 1. Peek at the whole table, first 5 rows
SELECT * FROM superstore LIMIT 5;

-- 2. Just the columns you care about
SELECT sub_category, sales, profit FROM superstore LIMIT 10;

-- 3. The distinct categories (like pandas .unique())
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM superstore;
```

`SELECT`/`FROM` is to SQL what `df[[...]]` is to pandas — choosing columns from a table.

cards.prompt: `SELECT` chooses which columns to return; `FROM` names the table.
cards.whenRight: Right — SELECT = columns, FROM = source table.
cards.whenWrong: It does — SELECT picks columns, FROM names the table they come from.

cards.prompt: `LIMIT 5` returns just the first 5 rows — a quick peek, like pandas .head().
cards.whenRight: Yes — LIMIT caps the rows returned; great for sanity checks.
cards.whenWrong: It is — LIMIT caps rows, the SQL equivalent of .head().

cards.prompt: `SELECT` can only return one column at a time.
cards.whenRight: Correct — list as many as you want, comma-separated, or `*` for all.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — SELECT takes a comma-separated list of columns (or * for all).
cards.sim: SELECT a, b, c FROM t;   -- many columns

days.title: WHERE — filter rows
days.summary: One concept: WHERE keeps the rows that match — SQL's version of a boolean mask — plus ORDER BY.

items.title: WHERE — filter rows
items.body:
## What it is
`WHERE` keeps only the rows that match a condition — exactly the pandas boolean mask, in words. `ORDER BY` sorts the result; `LIMIT` caps it.

## Why it matters
Analysis is filtering to the rows that answer the question — unprofitable orders, one region, big losses. WHERE is how you do that in SQL.

## Examples
```sql
-- 1. Only the loss-making orders
SELECT * FROM superstore WHERE profit < 0;

-- 2. Combine conditions with AND / OR (words, not & |)
SELECT * FROM superstore
WHERE region = 'East' AND sales > 500;

-- 3. The 10 biggest losses: filter, sort, cap
SELECT order_id, sub_category, profit
FROM superstore
WHERE profit < 0
ORDER BY profit ASC
LIMIT 10;
```

In pandas you wrote `df[df["profit"] < 0]`; in SQL it's `WHERE profit < 0`. Same idea, different syntax.

cards.prompt: `WHERE profit < 0` keeps only rows where profit is negative — like a pandas mask.
cards.whenRight: Right — WHERE is the SQL boolean filter.
cards.whenWrong: It does — WHERE is exactly the SQL version of a boolean mask.

cards.prompt: In SQL you combine two conditions with the words `AND` / `OR`.
cards.whenRight: Yes — SQL uses AND/OR words (pandas used & and | with parentheses).
cards.whenWrong: It does — SQL uses AND/OR, unlike pandas' & and |.

cards.prompt: `ORDER BY profit ASC` sorts from the largest profit down to the smallest.
cards.whenRight: Correct — ASC is ascending (smallest first); use DESC for largest first.
cards.whenWrong: Backwards — ASC is smallest-first; DESC is largest-first.
cards.sim: ORDER BY profit ASC  ->  biggest losses on top

days.title: GROUP BY — summarise into groups
days.summary: One concept: GROUP BY + SUM/AVG — the pivot table of SQL. Rewrite Q1 (margin leaders).

items.title: GROUP BY — summarise into groups
items.body:
## What it is
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group, paired with an **aggregate** (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`). It is the SQL pivot table — and the pandas `groupby` you already know.

## Why it matters
"Profit per sub-category", "sales per region" — every per-X question is a GROUP BY. This is the workhorse of analytical SQL.

## Examples
```sql
-- 1. Total profit per sub-category (Q1: margin leaders)
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
ORDER BY total_profit DESC;

-- 2. Several aggregates at once
SELECT category,
       SUM(sales)  AS revenue,
       AVG(profit) AS avg_profit,
       COUNT(*)    AS orders
FROM superstore
GROUP BY category;

-- 3. HAVING filters GROUPS after aggregating (WHERE filters rows before)
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
HAVING SUM(profit) < 0;     -- only loss-making sub-categories
```

cards.prompt: `GROUP BY sub_category` with `SUM(profit)` returns one total-profit row per sub-category.
cards.whenRight: Right — group, aggregate, one row out per group. The SQL pivot.
cards.whenWrong: It does — GROUP BY + an aggregate yields one summarised row per group.

cards.prompt: `HAVING` filters groups AFTER aggregation, while `WHERE` filters rows before it.
cards.whenRight: Yes — WHERE = rows pre-aggregation, HAVING = groups post-aggregation.
cards.whenWrong: Correct distinction — WHERE filters rows first, HAVING filters the grouped results.

cards.prompt: You can freely SELECT a raw column that's neither in GROUP BY nor inside an aggregate.
cards.whenRight: Correct — every selected column must be grouped or aggregated, or SQL errors.
cards.whenWrong: Not allowed — non-grouped, non-aggregated columns are ambiguous and error out.
cards.sim: GROUP BY category; SELECT sub_category -> error

items.body:

days.title: Aggregate over time (year-over-year)
days.summary: One concept: group by a slice of a date to get a trend — Q2 (YoY) in SQL.

items.title: Aggregate over time (year-over-year)
items.body:
## What it is
To see a trend you group by a **slice of the date**. In SQLite, `strftime('%Y', order_date)` pulls the year out, and you GROUP BY that.

## Why it matters
"Is the business growing?" is a time question. Grouping by year (or month) turns a pile of orders into a trend line — the Q2 year-over-year answer.

## Examples
```sql
-- 1. Yearly sales
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS yr,
       SUM(sales) AS revenue
FROM superstore
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;

-- 2. Sales AND profit per year, side by side
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS yr,
       SUM(sales)  AS revenue,
       SUM(profit) AS profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;
```

Read the rows top to bottom: is revenue climbing year over year? By how much?

cards.prompt: Grouping by the year pulled from a date gives one total per year — a trend.
cards.whenRight: Right — extract the year, GROUP BY it, and each row is one year's total.
cards.whenWrong: It does — grouping on the extracted year yields a per-year trend.

cards.prompt: `GROUP BY` only works on text columns, never on values derived from a date.
cards.whenRight: Correct — you can group by any expression, including a year extracted from a date.
cards.whenWrong: Not true — you can GROUP BY a derived value like strftime('%Y', date).

items.title: Top customers (CLV in SQL)
items.body:
## What it is
The CLV you computed in pandas last week is a single SQL query: group by the customer, sum their profit, sort, and cap.

## Why it matters
This is the payoff of learning the same idea in two tools — you'll *see* that pandas `groupby` and SQL `GROUP BY` express the identical logic. That transfer is what makes you tool-fluent, not tool-dependent.

## Examples
```sql
-- 1. Top 10 customers by lifetime profit
SELECT customer_name,
       SUM(profit) AS clv,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
FROM superstore
GROUP BY customer_name
ORDER BY clv DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Compare this list to your pandas result from Week 4 — it should match exactly. Same data, same logic, different language.

cards.prompt: Top-10 customers = GROUP BY customer, SUM(profit), ORDER BY DESC, LIMIT 10.
cards.whenRight: Right — that one query is CLV plus a leaderboard.
cards.whenWrong: It is — group, sum, sort, cap: the whole top-customers query.
cards.sim:
GROUP BY customer_name
ORDER BY clv DESC LIMIT 10

cards.prompt: pandas `groupby` and SQL `GROUP BY` express the same underlying idea.
cards.whenRight: Yes — split-apply-combine in both; only the syntax differs.
cards.whenWrong: They do — both are split-apply-combine; the logic is identical.
cards.sim:
pandas: groupby('cust')['profit'].sum()
SQL: GROUP BY customer SUM(profit)

## What it is
Collect every query you wrote this week into one file, `queries.sql`, each with a short comment saying what it answers.

## Why it matters
A saved, commented `.sql` file is a **deliverable**: anyone can rerun it against the data and get the same answers. Ad-hoc queries you typed and lost are not analysis — reproducible ones are.

## Examples
```sql
-- Q1: Margin leaders and laggards
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore GROUP BY sub_category ORDER BY total_profit DESC;

-- Q2: Year-over-year revenue
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS yr, SUM(sales) AS revenue
FROM superstore GROUP BY yr ORDER BY yr;

-- Q3: Top 10 customers by lifetime profit
SELECT customer_name, SUM(profit) AS clv
FROM superstore GROUP BY customer_name ORDER BY clv DESC LIMIT 10;
```

mastery_questions: Write Query 1: total Sales, Profit, and Profit Margin by Category. Use a CTE to compute the aggregates first: WITH cat_totals AS (SELECT Category, SUM(Sales) as total_sales, SUM(Profit) as total_profit FROM superstore GROUP BY Category) SELECT *, ROUND(total_profit * 1.0 / total_sales, 4) as margin FROM cat_totals ORDER BY margin DESC. Paste the result. Does it match the week-1 Excel pivot? If not, write which cells differ and why.

Write Query 2: annual revenue with year-over-year growth using a self-join. WITH annual AS (SELECT strftime('%Y', "Order Date") as year, SUM(Sales) as revenue FROM superstore GROUP BY 1) SELECT a.year, a.revenue, ROUND((a.revenue - b.revenue) * 1.0 / b.revenue, 4) as yoy_growth FROM annual a LEFT JOIN annual b ON CAST(a.year AS INT) = CAST(b.year AS INT) + 1 ORDER BY a.year. Paste the result. Does the YoY growth match weeks 1 and 2? Write one sentence about what the LEFT JOIN handles that an INNER JOIN would not.

Write Query 3: customer lifetime value -- total Profit, order count, and average order value per customer, sorted by total Profit descending, with LIMIT 10. Paste the top 10 customers and confirm the top customer's profit matches the week-4 customer aggregation. Now write Query 4: the segment distribution using a CASE statement to assign VIP/High/Medium/Low based on the NTILE(10) window function. Paste the query and the segment counts.

Write Query 5: the discount bucket analysis using a CASE statement equivalent to the nested IF from week 3. Add a GROUP BY on the bucket and Category. Paste the result confirming the margin at each discount bucket matches the week-3 analysis. Write one sentence about when you would use a CASE statement versus a lookup table join for binning a continuous variable.

Add a validation query for each of the four main queries: a simpler aggregation that checks the grand total. For example: SELECT SUM(total_profit) FROM (your margin query) should equal SELECT SUM(Profit) FROM superstore. Write and run all four validation queries. Paste their output. Validation queries are the SQL equivalent of the manual spot-check you did in week 1 -- every analyst who works in SQL should have this as a reflex.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the self-join year-over-year query -- the syntax for joining a table to itself with a year offset is mechanical and Claude writes it correctly. Verify the output against weeks 1 and 2. Do NOT use Claude to debug wrong query results. Debugging SQL requires understanding what data each clause produces -- use SELECT to inspect intermediate CTEs one at a time.
weeks.pre_flight: Install DB Browser for SQLite (free, cross-platform) and import the Superstore CSV into a new SQLite database. Run SELECT * FROM superstore LIMIT 5 and paste the output. Confirm the column names match what you expect from the CSV. If the column names have spaces (they do -- "Order Date", "Customer Name"), you will need to quote them with backticks or brackets in every query. Write that reminder at the top of queries.sql.
common_mistakes: Using integer division in SQLite. In SQLite, 1/3 returns 0, not 0.333. Always cast at least one operand to float: 1.0/3 or CAST(numerator AS REAL) / denominator. The most common manifestation: computing margin as Profit/Sales returns 0 for all rows because both are stored as integers.

Forgetting to quote column names with spaces. "Order Date" without quotes fails with "no such column: Order". Use backticks in SQLite: `Order Date`. Include a comment at the top of queries.sql reminding yourself of this -- it will save 20 minutes of debugging when you return to the file.

Writing SELECT * in production-style queries. SELECT * is fine for exploration, but every query in queries.sql should name its output columns explicitly. A query that returns unknown columns is a query that breaks silently when the source schema changes.

Not testing each query result against the corresponding Excel or Python output. The point of the SQL version is reproducibility -- if the numbers differ, you have a bug in one of the three versions and you need to find it.

Using subqueries where CTEs would be clearer. A query with three levels of nested subqueries is correct but unreadable. Refactor to CTEs before committing. Code that nobody can read in six months -- including you -- is technical debt.
weeks.debug_help: If a query returns unexpected results, use SELECT COUNT(*) to check row counts at each intermediate step. If a JOIN produces more rows than you expect, you probably have a many-to-many join -- check that the join key is unique on at least one side. If a GROUP BY returns fewer rows than you expect, you might have NULLs in the group column -- SQLite groups NULLs together as a single group, which can surprise you. Run SELECT "column_name", COUNT(*) FROM superstore GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 for any suspicious column and check whether NULL appears in the output.
stretch: Translate the queries to BigQuery SQL syntax (free tier available). The main differences: backtick quoting is the same, but date functions use DATE_TRUNC instead of strftime, and CAST uses a different syntax. Running the same queries in BigQuery proves they work against a production-grade engine.

Write a query that identifies customers who placed orders in 2016 but not in 2017 (churned customers) using a NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE IS NULL pattern. Churn identification in SQL is a standard analyst skill and this dataset is a clean example.

Write one stored view: CREATE VIEW customer_segments AS (your segment query). Then write a query on top of the view: SELECT * FROM customer_segments WHERE segment = 'VIP'. Views are the SQL equivalent of a named range in Excel -- they hide complexity and make downstream queries readable.

weeks.title: Statistical thinking for analysts
weeks.context:
Everything you found in weeks 1 through 5 is a pattern. Patterns are not findings. A finding is a pattern with evidence that it is real and not noise. "Furniture margins are lower than Technology margins" is a pattern. "Furniture margins are 7.2 percentage points lower than Technology margins (95% CI: 5.8 to 8.6 pp, p < 0.001)" is a finding you can defend.

Most business analysts never learn this distinction formally, which means most business analyses are underpowered. Someone presents "the West region grew 4% faster than the East" without asking whether 4% is a real difference or whether it would disappear with a different time window. Statisticians call this the file-drawer problem -- the analyses that do not show a significant result get quietly put away, and the ones that show a positive result get presented, regardless of how noisy the signal is.

This week you upgrade every finding from weeks 1 through 5 with appropriate statistical support. Confidence intervals around mean profit margin by Category. A t-test comparing VIP customer order values to Low Value customer order values. The Pearson correlation between Discount and Profit with a p-value. And a check for Simpson's paradox -- whether an aggregate finding reverses when you break it down by a subgroup.

Simpson's paradox is worth a specific example. If Technology has the best overall margin but the worst margin in the West region, the aggregate finding is misleading for the West region sales team. Any recommendation based on "Technology is our best category" could lead the West team to push the exact subcategory where they are losing money. Checking for reversal is not optional when regional or segment breakdowns exist.

By Sunday: every key finding in the Superstore analysis upgraded with a confidence interval or p-value, Simpson's paradox check documented for at least one finding, and the analyst memo updated to reflect the statistical framing.

days.title: Samples and selection bias
days.summary: A pattern in a biased sample is not a finding. Today: what your data does and doesn't represent.

items.title: Samples and selection bias
items.body:
## What it is
Your data is almost always a **sample**, not the whole population. **Selection bias** is when that sample isn't representative — so patterns in it may not hold in the real world.

## Why it matters
"Patterns are not findings." A finding is a pattern with evidence it's *real* and *generalisable*. If your sample is skewed, even a strong pattern can be an artefact of *who got into the data*.

## Examples
```text
- Survivorship bias: you only see customers who CHECKED OUT, not the carts abandoned.
- Self-selection: people who leave reviews are happier OR angrier than average.
- Coverage: Superstore is ONE retailer's orders — not "US retail" in general.
```

Before trusting any pattern, ask: *who or what is missing from this data, and would including them change the story?*

cards.prompt: A strong pattern in a biased sample may not hold in the wider population.
cards.whenRight: Right — bias in the sample can manufacture or hide patterns.
cards.whenWrong: It can mislead — a biased sample's pattern needn't generalise.
cards.sim: sample: only checkouts  ->  'everyone buys!' (abandoned carts unseen)

cards.prompt: Collecting more data automatically removes selection bias.
cards.whenRight: Correct — more biased data is just more bias. Representativeness, not volume, is the fix.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — volume doesn't fix bias; a bigger skewed sample is still skewed.

days.title: Confidence intervals
days.summary: One concept: report a range, not a falsely precise point. A single average hides uncertainty.

items.title: Confidence intervals
items.body:
## What it is
A single number — "average margin = 7.2%" — hides uncertainty. A **confidence interval (CI)** gives a range that probably contains the true value (commonly 95% confidence). Less data → wider interval.

## Why it matters
"Margins are 7.2% lower" sounds exact. "Margins are 7.2% lower, 95% CI [3.1%, 11.3%]" is honest — and if a difference's CI crosses zero, you can't claim the difference is real.

## Examples
```python
import numpy as np
x = df.loc[df["sub_category"] == "Tables", "profit"]

mean = x.mean()
se   = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))     # standard error
ci   = (mean - 1.96 * se, mean + 1.96 * se)  # ~95% CI
print(round(mean, 2), ci)
```

In Excel: `CONFIDENCE.NORM(0.05, stdev, n)` gives the +/- margin around the mean.

cards.prompt: A 95% CI is a range that likely contains the true value — not a guarantee it does.
cards.whenRight: Right — it quantifies uncertainty; it isn't a promise.
cards.whenWrong: Close — it's a likely range, not a certainty about the true value.

cards.prompt: A bigger sample makes the confidence interval narrower.
cards.whenRight: Yes — more data shrinks the standard error, tightening the interval.
cards.whenWrong: It does — larger n shrinks the standard error and narrows the CI.

cards.prompt: If a difference's 95% CI is [-2%, +9%], the difference is definitely positive.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the interval crosses zero, so 'no difference' is still plausible.
cards.whenWrong: Not definite — a CI spanning zero means the true difference could be zero or negative.

days.title: Correlation
days.summary: One concept: r — quantify the strength and direction of a relationship instead of eyeballing it.

items.title: Correlation
items.body:
## What it is
**Correlation (r)** measures how strongly two numeric variables move together, on a scale from **-1 to +1**. +1 = perfect upward line, -1 = perfect downward, 0 = no linear relationship.

## Why it matters
In Week 3 you *eyeballed* discount vs profit on a scatter. Correlation puts a number on it, so "they're related" becomes "r = -0.46, a moderate negative relationship."

## Examples
```python
# 1. Correlation between two columns
df["Discount"].corr(df["Profit"])      # e.g. -0.46

# 2. A correlation matrix across several numeric columns
df[["Discount", "Profit", "Sales", "Quantity"]].corr()
```

In Excel: `=CORREL(discount_range, profit_range)`. Read the sign (direction) and the magnitude (strength): |r| near 1 is strong, near 0 is weak.

cards.prompt: Correlation r runs from -1 to +1, and a value near 0 means little linear relationship.
cards.whenRight: Right — sign is direction, magnitude is strength; ~0 means weak/none.
cards.whenWrong: It does — r is bounded -1..+1, and near 0 means almost no linear link.

cards.prompt: r = -0.8 indicates a strong negative relationship between the two variables.
cards.whenRight: Yes — the sign is negative and |0.8| is large, so it's strong and downward.
cards.whenWrong: It is — negative sign, large magnitude = strong negative relationship.
cards.sim: as x up -> y down, tightly

cards.prompt: A high correlation proves that one variable causes the other.
cards.whenRight: Correct — correlation measures association only; causation needs more (tomorrow's lesson).
cards.whenWrong: Careful — high r is association, not proof of cause.

days.title: Correlation is not causation
days.summary: One concept: a confounder can drive two variables at once. Always ask 'what else explains this?'

items.title: Correlation is not causation
items.body:
## What it is
Two variables moving together doesn't mean one **causes** the other. Often a hidden third variable — a **confounder** — drives both.

## Why it matters
Your Week 3 finding ("high discounts -> losses") is correlational. Maybe discounts cause losses — or maybe clearance items that were *already* low-margin get the big discounts. Same correlation, very different action. Asking "what else could explain this?" is what separates an analyst from a chart-maker.

## Examples
```text
Classic: ice-cream sales correlate with shark attacks.
         Neither causes the other -> the confounder is SUMMER (hot weather).

Superstore: big discounts correlate with losses.
         Possible confounder: overstocked, low-margin items get the deepest cuts.
```

cards.prompt: Correlation between two variables alone proves one causes the other.
cards.whenRight: Correct — association is not causation; a confounder can drive both.
cards.whenWrong: It doesn't — correlation never proves cause on its own.

cards.prompt: A confounder is a hidden variable that influences both correlated variables.
cards.whenRight: Right — it creates the correlation without either causing the other.
cards.whenWrong: It is — a confounder drives both, faking a direct link.
cards.sim: summer -> ice cream AND -> beach crowds -> shark attacks

days.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
days.summary: One concept: a p-value tells you whether a gap is signal or could just be noise.

items.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
items.body:
## What it is
"Furniture margin < Technology margin" — is that a real difference or just random noise in this sample? A **hypothesis test** (e.g. a t-test) returns a **p-value**: the probability of seeing a gap this big if there were truly *no* difference.

## Why it matters
A small p-value (commonly < 0.05) means the gap is unlikely to be noise — worth acting on. A large p-value means you don't have enough evidence. This is how you stop over-reading random wiggles.

## Examples
```python
from scipy import stats
furn = df.loc[df["Category"] == "Furniture", "profit"]
tech = df.loc[df["Category"] == "Technology", "profit"]

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(furn, tech, equal_var=False)
print(f"p = {p:.4f}")     # p < 0.05  ->  difference unlikely to be noise
```

In Excel: `=T.TEST(rangeA, rangeB, 2, 3)`.

cards.prompt: A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) suggests the observed difference is unlikely to be just noise.
cards.whenRight: Right — low p = the gap would be rare if there were truly no difference.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a small p-value is evidence the difference is real, not random.
cards.sim: p = 0.003  ->  difference unlikely to be chance

cards.prompt: A p-value above 0.05 proves there is no difference between the groups.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it means insufficient evidence, not proof of 'no difference'.
cards.whenWrong: Not proof — high p means you can't conclude a difference, not that none exists.

days.title: Simpson's paradox
days.summary: One concept: an aggregate trend can reverse inside subgroups — always check the breakdown.

items.title: Simpson's paradox
items.body:
## What it is
**Simpson's paradox**: a trend that appears in aggregated data can **disappear or reverse** when you split into subgroups (and vice versa).

## Why it matters
"Discounts barely dent profit on average" can be flat-out wrong once you split by category — exactly what you saw in Week 3 Day 4, where Furniture bled while Technology shrugged it off. The aggregate lied; the subgroups told the truth. This is *why* you always break down.

## Examples
```text
Overall:   bigger discounts ~ only slightly lower profit   (looks fine)
By category:
   Furniture   -> profit collapses past 20% discount
   Technology  -> barely affected
=> the 'fine' average hid a category losing money.
```

cards.prompt: A trend in aggregated data can reverse when you split the data into subgroups.
cards.whenRight: Right — that reversal is Simpson's paradox in one line.
cards.whenWrong: It can — combining groups can flip or hide the within-group trend.

cards.prompt: Routinely checking subgroups protects you from Simpson's paradox.
cards.whenRight: Yes — breaking down by the relevant dimension is the standard guard.
cards.whenWrong: It does — subgroup checks are exactly how you catch a misleading aggregate.

resources.note: 7 min. Why running 10 tests guarantees 1 false positive. The fix.

resources.label: Spurious Correlations gallery
resources.note: Reference. Cheese consumption vs deaths by bedsheet. Hilarious and instructive.

exercises: Compute CIs for ALL pivot rows
Plot a confidence band on the monthly trend chart
Find one Simpson's paradox in HR data too
questions: Why isn't a correlation of 0.8 enough to claim causation?
What's a confound?
When does a junior analyst confuse association with causation?
mastery_questions: Compute a 95% confidence interval for the mean Profit Margin by Category. In Excel: =CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, STDEV(profit_margins), COUNT(profit_margins)) gives the margin of error; the CI is mean ± that value. Paste the CI for each Category. Write one sentence about whether the CIs for Technology and Furniture overlap -- if they do, the difference in sample means may not be statistically reliable.

Run a two-sample t-test comparing order profit between VIP customers and Low Value customers. In Excel: =T.TEST(vip_profits, low_profits, 2, 3) (two-tailed, two-sample unequal variance). Paste the p-value. Is p < 0.05? Write one sentence interpreting the result in plain English: not "p < 0.05 so it is significant" but "there is less than a 5% probability of observing a difference this large if VIPs and Low Value customers had identical average order profits."

Compute the Pearson correlation between Discount and Profit, and its p-value, using Excel's =CORREL() and =PEARSON(). For the p-value: =T.DIST.2T(r*SQRT(n-2)/SQRT(1-r^2), n-2) where r is the correlation and n is the count. Paste r and p. Is the correlation statistically significant? Write one sentence about practical versus statistical significance -- a significant correlation of -0.12 means discounts reliably decrease profit, but the effect explains only 1.4% of the variance.

Check for Simpson's paradox in the Discount-Margin relationship. Overall, higher discounts correlate with lower margins. Now compute the correlation separately for each Category. Is the direction consistent across all three? Write the three category-specific correlations. If one category has a positive correlation (more discount = better margin, perhaps because high-discount orders in that category are large bulk orders with better per-unit economics), that is Simpson's paradox and it changes the policy recommendation.

Update the analyst memo to add statistical framing to every key number. Replace "Furniture margins are lower" with "Furniture margins are 7.2 pp lower (95% CI: 5.8 to 8.6 pp)." Replace "VIP customers order more often" with "VIP customers place 14.2 orders per year versus 2.1 for Low Value customers (t=8.4, p<0.001)." Paste three revised sentences. A memo that says "significantly lower" without a number is a memo that has borrowed statistical authority it has not earned.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the p-value formula for a Pearson correlation in Excel -- it is derived from the t-distribution and is not built in as a single function. Paste the formula, verify it produces a plausible p-value (should be very small for a correlation of -0.4 with 5000 observations), and document it in queries.sql as a comment. Do NOT ask Claude whether a finding is statistically significant. That determination requires the actual data and the actual test result, not a language model's assessment.
weeks.pre_flight: For each of the three main findings from weeks 1-3, write down your confidence in the finding on a scale of 1-5 before running any statistical tests. After running the tests, update the scores. The gap between your prior confidence and the statistical evidence is calibration -- the analysts who are well-calibrated are the ones who can be trusted to say "I am not sure" when they are not sure.
common_mistakes: Reporting p < 0.05 without reporting the effect size. A tiny effect can be statistically significant with enough data. A large effect can be statistically insignificant with too little data. Always report both: the correlation and the p-value, or the mean difference and the confidence interval.

Interpreting a confidence interval as "the true value is definitely in this range." A 95% CI means that if you ran this analysis 100 times with different random samples, 95 of the resulting CIs would contain the true value. The one CI you computed may be one of the 5 that does not.

Reporting "correlation = 0.35 (p < 0.05)" without noting that r² = 0.12 -- discounts explain only 12% of the variance in profit. The percentage of variance explained is the most intuitive measure of practical importance for a correlation.

Not checking assumptions before running a t-test. The two-sample t-test assumes approximately normal distributions in each group. For profit data with extreme values (the $400K fare equivalent in retail is a very large bulk order), the normality assumption is violated. Note this as a limitation if sample sizes are small.

Using the same data to discover a finding and to test it. If you found the Furniture-margin pattern by exploring the data, testing it on the same data produces an inflated p-value. Ideally, you would reserve a holdout portion of the data for confirmatory testing. Acknowledging this limitation in the memo is the honest thing to do.
weeks.debug_help: Excel's T.TEST function arguments are easy to confuse: the third argument is tails (1 = one-tailed, 2 = two-tailed) and the fourth is type (1 = paired, 2 = two-sample equal variance, 3 = two-sample unequal variance). For comparing VIP and Low Value profits, use type=3 (Welch's t-test) because the variances are likely different. Using type=2 when variances differ produces an inflated p-value. Check: if the standard deviations of the two groups differ by more than a factor of 2, use type=3.
stretch: Run a one-way ANOVA to test whether mean Profit Margin differs significantly across the four Regions. Excel's Data Analysis ToolPak has a built-in ANOVA function. Report the F-statistic and p-value. If significant, run Tukey post-hoc tests to identify which specific pairs of regions differ significantly.

Compute the Spearman rank correlation between Discount and Profit as a robustness check on the Pearson correlation. If Spearman and Pearson give very different results, the outliers in the data are driving the Pearson correlation and the Spearman result is more reliable.

Read "Statistics Done Wrong" by Alex Reinhart (free online, 3 hours). Chapter 4 on p-values and Chapter 5 on data snooping are the two most relevant to business analysis. The book makes the case that most published statistics are overstated, and the reasons are exactly the errors listed in common mistakes above.

weeks.title: AI-Augmented analyst + Prompt Engineering
weeks.context:
Every analyst you will compete with for jobs has access to Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The ones who use AI well will be more productive. The ones who use it carelessly will produce confident-sounding wrong answers that are embarrassing to defend. This week you learn to be the first kind.

The discipline is verification. AI is genuinely excellent at generating SQL, writing formula syntax, drafting memo templates, and suggesting chart types. It is unreliable at interpreting data it cannot see, making business judgements that require domain knowledge, and catching subtle errors in analysis. Knowing which tasks to outsource and which to keep is the skill -- and it is a skill you practise by deliberately testing AI outputs against your own analysis this week.

The specific workflows you will build: a schema-aware SQL prompt (you paste the CREATE TABLE statement plus a question, AI generates the query, you run it and verify the output), a memo draft-and-critique loop (you paste your findings in bullet points, AI drafts a memo, you edit for accuracy and voice), and a formula generation prompt (you describe the logic in plain English, AI generates the Excel formula, you verify with spot checks).

The prompts.md file is the deliverable. Not the analysis -- you have already done the analysis. The deliverable is a documented set of prompts that work reliably for your analytical workflow, with notes on what each prompt is good for and where it fails. This is your personal AI cheatsheet, and it compounds over time: the better you get at prompting for analysis tasks, the more you can outsource the mechanical parts and spend your time on the parts that require actual thinking.

By Sunday: prompts.md committed to the Superstore repo with at least five working prompts, each with a "use for / not for" annotation, and one documented example where AI produced a wrong answer and you caught it.

days.title: AI accelerates, you stay accountable
days.summary: The one rule of AI-assisted analysis: it drafts, you verify. You own every number.

items.title: AI accelerates, you stay accountable
items.body:
## What it is
Every analyst you'll compete with has Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The edge isn't *using* AI — it's using it **well**: let it draft, then **you verify against the data**. You remain accountable for every number you ship.

## Why it matters
Careless AI use produces confident, wrong answers that are humiliating to defend in a meeting. Skilled use makes you 2-3x faster *without* sacrificing trust. The difference is verification.

## Examples
```text
Bad:   "ChatGPT said discounts cause 30% of losses" -> you can't defend it.
Good:  AI drafts the SQL -> you RUN it -> the number matches your own check
       -> you ship it and can explain every step.
```

cards.prompt: AI can produce confident-sounding but wrong answers, so you must verify its output against the data.
cards.whenRight: Right — fluency is not accuracy; verification is non-negotiable.
cards.whenWrong: It can — AI sounds sure even when wrong, so always verify.

cards.prompt: If the AI's answer sounds confident and detailed, you can trust it without checking.
cards.whenRight: Correct — confidence is not evidence. Run it, check it against the data.
cards.whenWrong: No — tone is not proof; verify against the actual data every time.

items.title: Your turn — honest assessment
items.body:
[WRITE] List two places AI could genuinely speed up your Superstore workflow.

[WRITE] List two places AI is risky (where a wrong-but-confident answer would bite you), and how you'd verify.

days.title: Schema-aware prompts for SQL
days.summary: AI writes great SQL only when you hand it the schema and the exact question — then you run it.

items.title: Schema-aware prompts for SQL
items.body:
## What it is
AI writes SQL fast, but only if you give it the **table schema** and a **precise question**. A vague prompt yields a plausible-but-wrong query.

## Why it matters
You already wrote these queries by hand in Week 5, so you can *verify* the AI — the perfect way to learn what good prompting looks like while staying safe.

## Examples
```text
Weak prompt:   "write SQL to find my best products"

Strong prompt: "Table superstore(order_id, sub_category, category,
                sales, profit, discount, order_date, customer_name).
                Write SQLite to return each sub_category's total profit,
                highest first."
```

Then **run it** in sqliteonline and confirm it matches your Week 5 answer.

cards.prompt: Giving the AI your exact table schema makes its SQL far more likely to be correct.
cards.whenRight: Right — column names + types remove the guessing that causes wrong queries.
cards.whenWrong: It does — schema-aware prompts dramatically cut wrong-column errors.

cards.prompt: AI-generated SQL can be trusted and shipped without running it.
cards.whenRight: Correct — always run it and check the result against a known answer.
cards.whenWrong: Never ship unrun — execute it and verify against data you trust.
cards.sim: AI SQL -> RUN -> compare to Week 5 -> then trust

items.title: Your turn — prompt, run, verify
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Write a schema-aware prompt asking an AI for the Q1 'profit per sub_category' query.

[CODE] Run the AI's SQL in sqliteonline.

[WRITE] One sentence: did it match your hand-written Week 5 result? If not, what did the AI get wrong?

days.title: AI as a memo drafter
days.summary: Feed AI your real numbers + audience; it drafts the prose; you edit for accuracy and voice.

items.title: AI as a memo drafter
items.body:
## What it is
Hand the AI **your** findings (the real numbers) plus the audience, and it drafts the memo prose in seconds. You then edit for accuracy, tone, and truth.

## Why it matters
Writing is the slow part; drafting is where AI shines. But it must build from *your* numbers — never let it invent figures, because invented numbers are how careers end.

## Examples
```text
Prompt: "Audience: a non-technical sales director.
         Findings: discounts above 30% turn the average order unprofitable;
         Furniture tips at 20%; ~18% of orders exceed these caps.
         Draft a 150-word memo: headline, evidence, recommendation."
Then: edit for your voice and DELETE anything you can't back with data.
```

cards.prompt: AI should draft the memo from YOUR numbers — it must not invent figures of its own.
cards.whenRight: Right — you supply the facts; AI supplies the phrasing. Verify nothing was fabricated.
cards.whenWrong: Exactly — AI phrases your facts; invented numbers are a firing offence.
cards.sim: you: the numbers  |  AI: the wording

items.title: Your turn — draft then edit
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Give an AI your real discount + CLV findings and ask for a 150-word memo for a non-technical director.

[WRITE] Edit the draft. Note two things you changed (a fabricated/ovestated claim removed, or voice fixed).

days.title: Make AI critique your memo
days.summary: Flip the tool: ask AI to attack your own memo for weak claims and missing caveats.

items.title: Make AI critique your memo
items.body:
## What it is
Paste your finished memo and ask the AI to **find its weaknesses** — unsupported claims, missing caveats, alternative explanations. A tireless, free critical reviewer.

## Why it matters
You're blind to your own gaps. An adversarial pass before your boss sees it catches the embarrassing holes while they're still cheap to fix. You decide which critiques are fair.

## Examples
```text
Prompt: "You are a skeptical data director. Find the 3 weakest claims in this
         memo and the questions I'd get grilled on. Be specific."
-> e.g. "You claim discounts CAUSE losses but only show correlation — address
   the confounder, or soften to 'associated with'."
```

cards.prompt: Asking AI to critique your own work surfaces gaps and weak claims you're blind to.
cards.whenRight: Right — an adversarial review pass is one of AI's highest-value uses.
cards.whenWrong: It does — AI as a skeptic catches holes before your audience does.
cards.sim: AI: 'claim 2 is correlation, not causation -> soften it'

items.title: Your turn — get grilled (safely)
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask an AI to act as a skeptical director and list the 3 weakest claims in your memo.

[WRITE] Address at least two of them in the memo (add a caveat, soften a claim, or add evidence).

days.title: AI for slide content
days.summary: Turn your memo into lean slide bullets and speaker notes — AI phrases, you keep it tight.

items.title: AI for slide content
items.body:
## What it is
Give the AI your memo and ask for **slide bullets + speaker notes**. It compresses prose into talking points so you can present, not read.

## Why it matters
Executives get a deck, not a notebook. Lean slides with strong speaker notes are how a finding actually lands in the room — and AI drafts them fast.

## Examples
```text
Prompt: "From this memo, draft 3 slides. For each: a 5-word title, 3 bullets
         (<=8 words each), and 2 sentences of speaker notes I can say aloud."
Then: cut every bullet that isn't essential. Slides are signposts, not scripts.
```

cards.prompt: AI can turn your memo into per-slide bullets and speaker notes you refine.
cards.whenRight: Right — it compresses prose to talking points; you keep it lean.
cards.whenWrong: It can — AI drafts slide content fast; your job is to trim it.

items.title: Your turn — deck-ify it
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask AI to convert your memo into 3 slides (title + 3 short bullets + 2 sentences of speaker notes each).

[WRITE] Trim the result: delete any bullet that isn't essential to the recommendation.

days.title: AI for tricky formulas and code
days.summary: Describe the calculation; AI writes the formula or pandas code; you verify on a known case.

items.title: AI for tricky formulas and code
items.body:
## What it is
Stuck on a gnarly Excel formula or a pandas one-liner? Describe what you want in plain English and the AI writes it. Then **test it on a row where you already know the answer**.

## Why it matters
This removes the syntax bottleneck — but unverified formulas silently produce wrong columns. The verify-on-a-known-case habit is what keeps AI speed from becoming AI risk.

## Examples
```text
Prompt: "pandas: add a year-over-year % growth column on yearly_sales
         (columns: year, revenue), sorted by year."
-> yearly["yoy"] = yearly["revenue"].pct_change() * 100
Verify: hand-check one year's % against the raw numbers.
```

cards.prompt: You should always test an AI-generated formula on a case where you already know the answer.
cards.whenRight: Right — a known-answer check is the cheapest guard against a silently-wrong formula.
cards.whenWrong: Always — verify on a known case before trusting an AI formula across the data.
cards.sim: AI formula -> check on 1 known row -> then apply

items.title: Your turn — generate and verify
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask AI for a formula/snippet you find fiddly (e.g. year-over-year % growth, or a running total).

[CODE] Apply it, then hand-verify the result on one row you can compute yourself.

days.title: Ship: AI-aware (prompts.md)
days.summary: Save your best prompts as reusable assets and tag AI-aware.

items.title: Ship: AI-aware (prompts.md)
items.body:
## What it is
Collect the prompts that actually worked this week into a `prompts.md` file — your reusable toolkit — and tag the project `AI-aware`.

## Why it matters
Good prompts are assets: you'll reuse the schema-aware SQL prompt and the skeptical-reviewer prompt on every future project. Saving them (and showing you verify AI output) signals deliberate, professional AI use — exactly what employers now screen for.

cards.prompt: Saving your effective prompts in a file turns them into reusable assets for future projects.
cards.whenRight: Right — a prompt library compounds; you stop reinventing them each time.
cards.whenWrong: It does — saved prompts are reusable tools, not one-offs.
cards.sim: prompts.md -> reuse the schema + critique prompts everywhere

items.title: Acceptance — AI-aware is done when
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Create `prompts.md` with your best prompts from this week (SQL generation, memo draft, skeptical critique, formula help), each with a one-line note on when to use it.

[WRITE] Add one line to your README on how you verified AI output (so reviewers know you didn't just trust it).

[CODE] Commit, tag `AI-aware`, push. Drop your repo link in the dashboard check-in.
